content: Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have indicated that delaying the initiation of parenteral nutrition (PN) may provide clinical advantages in critically ill adults and children. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the optimal timing for starting PN in critically ill term and late preterm infants. The objective of this study was to assess the benefits and safety of initiating PN early versus late in critically ill term and late preterm infants. Early PN was defined as starting within 72 hours of admission, while late PN was defined as starting after 72 hours of admission. Term infants were defined as those born at 37 weeks of gestation or later, and late preterm infants were defined as those born between 34 weeks and 36 weeks plus 6 days of gestation. A comprehensive search was conducted using Cochrane Neonatal's standard search strategy across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, EMCare, and PubMed, up to April 5, 2019. Additional searches were performed for ongoing or recently completed clinical trials, grey literature, and reference lists of relevant publications. The inclusion criteria for this review were RCTs that compared early versus late initiation of PN in term and late preterm infants. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Treatment effects were reported as risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Two RCTs met the inclusion criteria, but data were only available from a subgroup of 209 term infants included in one RCT. This trial, conducted in Belgium, the Netherlands, and Canada, involved children from birth to 17 years of age who were at medium to high risk of malnutrition and expected to stay in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for at least 24 hours. In this study, early PN was defined as initiation within 24 hours of admission, while late PN was defined as initiation after the seventh day of admission to the PICU. The risk of bias in this study was considered low for five domains but high for two domains. Among the subgroup of term infants, those who received late PN had a significantly lower risk of in-hospital all-cause mortality (RR 0.35, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.14 to 0.87; RD -0.10, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.02; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] = 10). Similarly, late PN was associated with a significantly lower risk of neonatal mortality (death from any cause within the first 28 days of life) (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.88; RD -0.09, 95% CI -0.16 to -0.01; NNTB = 11). There were no significant differences between the early and late PN groups in terms of rates of healthcare-associated bloodstream infections, growth parameters, or duration of hospital stay. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in the included studies. The quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as low due to imprecision (resulting from the small sample size and wide confidence intervals) and a high risk of bias in the included studies. In conclusion, while late initiation of PN in term and late preterm infants may offer some benefits, the low quality of the evidence limits confidence in these findings. Further adequately powered RCTs are needed to evaluate both short-term and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
